blocks.title: Machines That Predict the Next Word
blocks.subtitle: Tokens, attention and the transformer

blocks.text:
A large language model does one thing: given some text, it estimates what comes next. Repeating that step, one token at a time, produces answers, essays, translations and computer code.

That such a simple objective yields such broad ability is one of the surprises of modern computing. Understanding the mechanism also makes the limits easier to see.

blocks.heading: From text to prediction
blocks.text: Text is split into **tokens**, each mapped to a vector of numbers. Layers of **self-attention** let every token gather information from the others in the context, building up a representation of meaning. The final layer converts that representation into a probability for every possible next token.

steps.text: **Tokenise.** The input is broken into sub-word pieces from a fixed vocabulary, so rare words can still be represented.
**Embed.** Each token becomes a vector, and position information is added so that word order is kept.
**Attend.** In every layer, attention weighs how much each token should draw on every other token.
**Predict.** The model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary, one token is chosen, and the loop repeats.

points.title: Tokeniser
points.text: Splits text into sub-word tokens and maps them to integer IDs.

points.title: Embeddings
points.text: A learned vector for each token, plus information about its position.

points.title: Transformer layers
points.text: Stacked attention and feed-forward blocks that refine the representation.

points.title: Output probabilities
points.text: A score for every token in the vocabulary, turned into probabilities.

points.title: Decoding
points.text: Sampling rules such as temperature and top-p that choose the next token.

blocks.heading: Training in two stages
blocks.text: In **pre-training**, the model reads a very large body of text and learns to predict hidden or following tokens. No labels are needed. In **fine-tuning** and alignment, it is further trained on examples of the behaviour wanted, such as following instructions helpfully and declining harmful requests. Additional information can be supplied at run time by retrieving documents and placing them in the context.

items.title: Token
items.text: The unit of text a model reads and writes; often a word fragment.

items.title: Attention
items.text: A mechanism that lets each position weigh the relevance of all others.

items.title: Context window
items.text: The maximum amount of text the model can consider at once.

blocks.text: A language model is trained to be plausible. Being correct is something its users must check.

blocks.heading: Using them well
blocks.text: Language models can state falsehoods confidently, reflect biases in their training text and miss recent events. Treat output as a draft: verify facts and citations, keep confidential data out of services you do not control, and keep a person responsible for decisions that matter. Evaluation on your own task is more informative than any general benchmark.

blocks.question: What is a large language model trained to do?
options: Look up facts in a database
Predict the next token given the preceding text
blocks.explanation: Next-token prediction on very large text collections is the core training objective.

blocks.question: What does 'retrieval-augmented generation' add?
options: Relevant documents placed in the context at run time
blocks.explanation: Retrieved passages give the model current, specific information to ground its answer.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Parameter**: a learned number in the network. **Prompt**: the text given to the model. **Temperature**: a setting that makes sampling more or less random. **Embedding**: a vector representing a token or passage. **Inference**: running a trained model.
